name: Vertex
quick: One of the objects in a graph, usually drawn as a labeled dot.
definition: A graph consists of objects and connections. A vertex is one of those objects; vertices is the plural. Its position in a drawing is chosen to make connections readable, not to assign a mathematical value. In the formal description $G=(V,E)$, $G$ names the graph, $V$ is its set of vertices, and $E$ is its set of edges, the connections between vertices.
example: If a graph models towns and direct roads, each town is a vertex. Four towns named a, b, c, and d give $V=\{a,b,c,d\}$.
confusion: A crossing of two drawn edges is not an additional vertex unless a dot explicitly marks it.
section: Relations as sets of ordered pairs

name: Edge
quick: A connection between two vertices in a graph.
definition: In a simple undirected graph an edge joins two distinct vertices. It is represented by an unordered pair $\{u,v\}$: exchanging the order does not change the connection. In a directed graph the order matters, so an arrow from u to v is represented by $(u,v)$.
example: An edge between a and b might represent a direct road. A route from a through c to b does not itself create the edge joining a and b.
confusion: Connected by a route and joined by one edge are different claims.
section: Relations as sets of ordered pairs

name: Graph
quick: A collection of vertices together with edges recording which vertices are connected.
definition: A graph records a pattern of connections. Our default is a finite simple undirected graph: finitely many vertices, edges with no direction, no edge from a vertex to itself, and at most one edge per pair of vertices. The notation $G=(V,E)$ names both the vertex set and edge set.
example: A triangle has three vertices and all three possible edges between them. Moving the dots leaves the same graph if those connections stay the same.
confusion: A graph in graph theory need not be the coordinate plot of a function.

name: Self-loop
quick: An edge that connects a vertex to itself.
definition: A self-loop begins and ends at the same vertex. A directed relation diagram can use it to show that an object is related to itself. The simple graph convention used in the graph-theory lesson excludes loops.
example: The pair $(a,a)$ in a relation is drawn as an arrow curving from a back to a.
confusion: A loop is different from a longer route that returns to its starting point.
section: Relations as sets of ordered pairs

name: Parallel edges
quick: Two or more distinct edges joining the same pair of vertices.
definition: Some models distinguish separate connections between the same objects. Such models can have parallel edges. A simple graph cannot: its edge set contains at most one unordered pair for those endpoints.
example: Two different bridges connecting the same islands are two connections in a bridge model, even though they join the same pair of islands.
confusion: The word parallel describes repeated endpoints here, not the geometric direction of drawn lines.

name: Directed graph
quick: A graph whose edges have a direction, indicated by arrows.
definition: A directed edge, also called an arc, is an ordered pair $(u,v)$. It permits travel from u to v. The opposite ordered pair $(v,u)$ is a different arc and need not be present. This course states explicitly whether a model permits loops.
example: A web page may link to another page that does not link back. Represent that one-way connection with one arrow.
confusion: Two opposite arrows are not the same as a single directed edge.
section: Relations as sets of ordered pairs

name: Adjacent vertices
quick: Vertices that are joined directly by an edge.
definition: Adjacency is a local relationship: one edge connects the two vertices. In an undirected graph the relationship works both ways. A neighbor of a vertex is another vertex adjacent to it.
example: In the edges ab, bc, ca, cd, vertex c is adjacent to a, b, and d, while a and d are not adjacent.
confusion: A path with several edges can connect vertices that are not adjacent.

name: Incident
quick: An edge is incident to a vertex when that vertex is one of its endpoints.
definition: Incidence describes an edge meeting a vertex. An ordinary undirected edge has two endpoints and is incident to both. It is a relationship between an edge and a vertex, unlike adjacency, which relates two vertices.
example: The edge $\{c,d\}$ is incident to c and to d.
confusion: Do not count crossings in the drawing as incidences unless they are marked vertices.

name: Degree
quick: The number of edges incident to a vertex in a simple undirected graph.
definition: To find a vertex’s degree, count the edges touching that vertex. Since our graph is simple, counting its distinct neighbors gives the same result. Write this number as $\deg(v)$. Every edge contributes one to each of its two endpoints, so summing all degrees counts every edge twice.
example: For edges ab, bc, ca, cd, c has degree 3 and d has degree 1. The four degrees sum to 8, twice the four edges.
confusion: Degree counts direct connections, not all vertices reachable by a route.

name: Isolated vertex
quick: A vertex with no incident edges; its degree is zero.
definition: An isolated vertex still belongs to the graph. It has no neighbors, so there is no way to leave it along an edge. It forms a connected component by itself.
example: Add a dot e with no edges to a triangle. The graph now has four vertices, not three.
confusion: A vertex drawn far from others is not necessarily isolated; look at its edges.

name: In-degree
quick: The number of directed edges arriving at a vertex.
definition: An incoming arc has the vertex as its second endpoint. Count each such arc once. Its outgoing arcs contribute instead to its out-degree. Over the entire digraph the in-degrees sum to the number of arcs.
example: With arrows a to c and b to c, c has in-degree 2.
confusion: A large in-degree does not imply a large out-degree.

name: Out-degree
quick: The number of directed edges leaving a vertex.
definition: An outgoing arc has the vertex as its first endpoint. Its direction determines which local count it contributes to. Summing out-degrees over all vertices counts each arc once.
example: If c points only to d, then c has out-degree 1, regardless of how many arrows arrive at c.
confusion: In-degree and out-degree measure different ends of each directed edge.

name: Walk
quick: A sequence of vertices in which every consecutive pair is joined by an edge.
definition: A walk records a route through a graph. It may repeat vertices and edges. Its length is the number of edges traversed, so a sequence of k+1 vertices describes k steps. In a directed graph each step must follow an arrow.
example: In the triangle a, b, c with an extra edge cd, a,b,c,a,c,d is a walk of length 5.
confusion: Before deciding whether a route is a special kind of walk, check that every requested edge exists.
section: Relations as sets of ordered pairs

name: Trail
quick: A walk that never uses the same edge twice.
definition: A trail restricts edge repetition but permits vertex repetition. In an undirected graph, using an edge in the reverse direction still uses the same edge. A closed trail ends where it began.
example: The route a,b,c,a around a triangle is a closed trail: each of its three edges appears once.
confusion: A trail need not be a path because it can revisit a vertex.

name: Path
quick: A walk with no repeated vertex, under this course’s convention.
definition: A path visits each of its listed vertices at most once. This rules out repeating an edge as well. A single vertex is a path of length zero. Other books sometimes use path for a broader type of walk; check the stated convention.
example: The route a,c,d is a path of length 2 when ac and cd are edges.
confusion: A route that returns to its starting vertex is not a path under this convention.

name: Cycle
quick: A route that returns to its start without repeating other vertices.
definition: For a simple undirected graph a cycle has at least three edges, its last vertex is its first, and all vertices before that final return are distinct. In a loop-free digraph, a directed cycle may have length two if opposite arcs are present.
example: The route a,b,c,a around a triangle is an undirected cycle.
confusion: Going along one undirected edge and immediately back repeats the edge and is not a cycle.

name: Connected graph
quick: A nonempty undirected graph in which a path joins every pair of vertices.
definition: Connectivity asks whether every vertex can be reached from every other by some route. Direct adjacency is unnecessary. Under this course’s convention a single vertex is connected, while the empty graph is disconnected.
example: A line of three vertices a—b—c is connected although no edge joins a directly to c.
confusion: Connected does not mean that every possible edge is present.

name: Connected component
quick: A connected part of a graph that cannot be enlarged while remaining connected.
definition: A component contains every vertex reachable from any one of its vertices, together with the edges between those vertices. Different components have no edges between them. Maximal means no additional vertex can be included, not largest by size.
example: A separate triangle and isolated dot form two components.
confusion: The smaller of two components is still maximal: adding a vertex from the other component would disconnect it.

name: Acyclic
quick: Containing no cycles.
definition: Acyclic describes the absence of cycles, rather than a particular visual shape. An undirected acyclic graph may have several separate pieces. A directed acyclic graph forbids directed cycles; its underlying undirected connections can still form a cycle.
example: The arrows a to b, a to c, and b to c have no directed cycle.
confusion: A drawing can look circular even when it has no directed cycle: check arrow directions.

name: Tree
quick: A nonempty connected undirected graph with no cycles.
definition: A tree connects all its vertices without any redundant cycle edge. Between any two vertices there is exactly one path. A tree with n vertices has n−1 edges, but that edge count by itself does not establish that an arbitrary graph is a tree.
example: The four-vertex edges ab, bc, and cd form a tree. A triangle plus an isolated dot has three edges too, but is not a tree.
confusion: A tree need not be drawn upright or have a designated root.

name: Forest
quick: An undirected graph with no cycles, possibly empty or disconnected.
definition: Every nonempty component of a forest is a tree. If a forest has n vertices and c components, it has n−c edges: each component with k vertices contributes k−1 edges.
example: Two disjoint edges form a forest with four vertices, two components, and two edges.
confusion: A forest does not have to be connected.

name: Root
quick: The chosen reference vertex of a rooted tree.
definition: Choosing one vertex as the root lets us describe the tree relative to it. Every other vertex has a parent: the preceding vertex on the unique path from the root. Children are vertices that have the given vertex as parent. Depth is the number of edges from the root.
example: In a chain r—a—b rooted at r, a is the parent of b and b has depth 2.
confusion: Changing the root changes parent relationships, not the underlying undirected edges.

name: Leaf
quick: In a rooted tree, a vertex with no children; in an unrooted tree, usually a vertex of degree 1.
definition: The two conventions serve different purposes. When parent-child relationships are specified, count children. In an ordinary unrooted tree, count incident edges. A one-vertex rooted tree has a leaf root.
example: A root with one child has degree 1 but is not a rooted-tree leaf.
confusion: Always check whether the tree is rooted before applying the word leaf.

name: Directed acyclic graph
quick: A directed graph with no directed cycles.
definition: The abbreviation DAG stands for directed acyclic graph. Such a graph can represent prerequisite tasks, with an arrow from a prerequisite to a task that depends on it. In a finite nonempty DAG at least one vertex has no incoming arcs.
example: The arrows a to c, b to c, and c to d have no directed cycle, so they form a DAG.
confusion: A directed graph is not acyclic merely because each individual arrow goes between distinct vertices.

name: Topological ordering
quick: An ordering of a digraph’s vertices in which each arrow points from earlier to later.
definition: A topological ordering respects all directed prerequisites. Finite DAGs admit such an ordering: repeatedly remove a vertex with no remaining incoming arcs. A directed cycle prevents any topological ordering.
example: For arrows a to c, b to c, and c to d, both a,b,c,d and b,a,c,d work.
confusion: The ordering need not be unique. Alphabetical order is only a tie-breaking rule if explicitly chosen.

name: Adjacency matrix
quick: A table whose entry records whether one vertex is joined to another.
definition: Use the same ordered list of vertices for rows and columns. An entry is 1 when the specified edge exists and 0 otherwise. For an undirected simple graph the matrix is symmetric and its diagonal is zero. For a digraph, row u and column v record the arc from u to v.
example: An undirected edge ab puts 1 in both row a/column b and row b/column a.
confusion: A symmetric table is required only for the undirected convention.

name: Adjacency list
quick: For each vertex, a list of the vertices it connects to directly.
definition: An undirected adjacency list records every edge at both endpoints. A directed outgoing-neighbor list records an arc only at its starting vertex. This representation uses space proportional to the number of vertices plus edges.
example: For edges ab, bc, ca, cd, the list for c is a,b,d.
confusion: A list of neighbors is not a list of all reachable vertices.

name: Queue
quick: A collection processed first in, first out.
definition: Adding an item to the back is called enqueueing. Removing the oldest waiting item from the front is dequeueing. Breadth-first search uses a queue so that earlier discovered vertices are processed first.
example: If a then b then c enter an empty queue, they leave in that order.
confusion: A queue is different from a stack, which removes the most recent item first.

name: Stack
quick: A collection processed last in, first out.
definition: A stack removes the most recently added item first. It can record unfinished work: after completing a deeper branch, return to the most recent unfinished branch. Depth-first search can use an explicit stack or the stack of recursive function calls.
example: If a then b then c are placed on a stack, c is removed first.
confusion: Using a stack instead of a queue changes traversal order, not the edges in the graph.

name: Breadth-first search
quick: A traversal that explores vertices in increasing edge-count distance from its start.
definition: BFS marks a vertex when first discovered and puts it in a queue. Processing a vertex examines its neighbors. This visits all distance-1 vertices before distance-2 vertices, and so on. A specified neighbor order resolves ties.
example: Starting at a in the graph ab, ac, bc, cd and scanning alphabetically discovers a,b,c,d with distances 0,1,1,2.
confusion: Minimum edge count is not minimum total weight when edges have unequal costs.

name: Depth-first search
quick: A traversal that follows an unvisited branch before returning to earlier unfinished branches.
definition: DFS marks visited vertices so cycles do not cause repeated exploration. It can be described recursively or implemented with a stack. A specified neighbor order is necessary when an exercise asks for one exact discovery sequence.
example: At a, choose its first unvisited neighbor, continue from there, and backtrack only when no unvisited neighbor remains.
confusion: DFS does not generally find shortest paths.

name: Euler trail
quick: A trail that uses every edge of the graph exactly once.
definition: Euler questions concern edges. Vertices may be revisited. A closed Euler trail is an Euler circuit. For an undirected graph with edges, the edge-bearing part must be connected; an open Euler trail has exactly two odd-degree vertices, while a circuit has none.
example: Traversing the four sides of a square returns to the start and uses each edge once: an Euler circuit.
confusion: An Euler trail need not visit each vertex only once.

name: Hamiltonian cycle
quick: A cycle that visits every vertex exactly once before returning to its start.
definition: Hamiltonian questions concern vertices. The cycle can leave many edges unused. Unlike Euler trails, its existence is not decided just by counting odd degrees.
example: The four sides of a square form a Hamiltonian cycle, even if both diagonals are also edges.
confusion: Do not apply the Euler parity criterion to decide whether a Hamiltonian cycle exists.
